subject: Climate & Environment
title: Climate-Resilient Infrastructure
description: A micro-lesson that makes Climate-Resilient Infrastructure usable.

hook.text: New York spent $20 billion on flood defenses after Hurricane Sandy. The next storm will be worse.

buildup.text: Resilient infrastructure is designed to absorb shocks — floods, heat, storms — and keep functioning.

discovery.text: Elevated roads, flood barriers, backup power systems, and redundant water supplies all build resilience.

twist.text: Spending $1 on resilience saves $6 in future disaster recovery costs on average.

climax.text: The cities that invest in resilience now will be the ones still standing in 2100.

punchline.text: Resilience isn't about preventing disaster. It's about surviving it.

quiz.question: How much does each dollar spent on resilience save in disaster recovery?

details.summary: Climate-resilient infrastructure is designed to withstand and recover from floods, heat waves, storms, and other climate impacts. It includes elevated roads, flood barriers, cooling systems, and redundant power and water networks that maintain essential services during extreme events.
details.whyItMatters: Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure saves several in avoided disaster damage. As extreme weather intensifies, cities that fail to adapt face escalating costs and disruption.
takeaways: Resilient design anticipates future climate conditions
Elevated and flood-proofed structures reduce damage costs
Redundant systems maintain services during extreme events

faq.question: What makes infrastructure climate resilient?
faq.answer: Resilient infrastructure is built to higher standards for heat, wind, and water. It includes elevated critical facilities, flood-proofed utilities, natural buffers like wetlands, backup power systems, and materials that withstand temperature extremes. Design accounts for future climate projections.

faq.question: How do cities decide which infrastructure to protect first?
faq.answer: Cities conduct vulnerability assessments to identify critical assets like hospitals, water treatment plants, and power grids that serve the most people. They prioritize investments based on exposure to climate hazards, population density, and socioeconomic vulnerability.
